paper.abstract: Abstract In the absence of ground truth, most existing infrared and visible image fusion methods pursue fidelity to the source images and directly superimpose two physically distinct modalities. As a result, salient infrared targets appear as bright patches of thermal radiation pasted onto the scene. These patches obscure the original color and texture of the targets, so the fused images look unnatural to human observers and deviate from the data distribution learned by vision models pretrained on visible images. Therefore, we redefine infrared and visible image fusion as natural complementary enhancement rather than source fidelity, and propose NatureFusion , which exploits cross-modal complementary cues to infer a clear and natural visible-style image from low-quality visible and infrared image pairs. Specifically, to address the lack of ground truth, we employ a generative foundation model as the teacher to directly generate visually natural fused images for supervision. Furthermore, to fully distill the teacher’s generative capability while reducing computational cost, we fine-tune a pretrained generative model with conditional flow matching through a light-weight fusion adapter. Last but not least, to further improve downstream performance without sacrificing natural appearance, we freeze the fusion adapter and introduce a detector-supervised task adapter that strengthens the complementary contribution of infrared. Extensive comparisons with seven multi-modal fusion and seven single-modality enhancement methods demonstrate that NatureFusion generates visually natural fused images with the best perceptual quality. Detection and segmentation models pretrained on visible images achieve substantially higher accuracy on our fused images than on those of any competing method.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Visible images capture the color and texture of a scene, but targets such as pedestrians are often difficult to recognize in poorly lit regions. Infrared images record thermal radiation from the scene and can highlight the locations of these targets, yet they lack color and texture details, as shown in Fig. 1 (a) and (b). Therefore, infrared and visible image fusion aims to combine the complementary information of the two modalities into a fused image that is better suited to observation and analysis, benefiting both human observers in applications such as in-vehicle night vision and vision models in downstream tasks such as object detection. Fig. 1: Comparison with multi-modal fusion and single-modality enhancement methods. Panels (a) and (b) show the visible and infrared inputs, (c) to (e) show the results of degradation-aware fusion, task-driven fusion, and single-modality enhancement methods, and (f) shows the result of NatureFusion. Red and blue boxes mark enlarged person and background regions, and gold boxes show person detections of a frozen RetinaNet with confidence scores of at least 0.25. (g) to (i) Comparison with seven multi-modal fusion methods in MUSIQ on M3FD, person AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} on SMOD, and mIoU 2 \mathrm{mIoU}_{2} over Car and Person on MFNet. Detection and segmentation each use seven frozen models pretrained on visible images. Bars show means, and whiskers show ranges across images and models. However, in the absence of ground truth specifying what an ideal fused image should look like, most existing infrared and visible image fusion methods follow a source-fidelity paradigm, which uses unsupervised intensity, structure, and gradient losses to keep the fused image faithful to the source images. Notably, this paradigm faces a critical challenge, namely that the two modalities are physically distinct. Infrared intensity reflects the thermal radiation of objects rather than their appearance under visible light, so a pedestrian in dark clothing can appear bright in the infrared image but dark in the visible image. When the fused image is forced to remain faithful to both modalities, such targets are highlighted as bright patches of thermal radiation that obscure their original color and texture, making the fused image unsuitable for both human observers and vision models, as shown in Fig. 1 (c) and (d). For human observers, these patches make the fused image look unnatural, especially in low-light and other degraded scenes, where weak visible signals leave the result dominated by thermal patterns. To cope with such scenes, degradation-aware methods incorporate image enhancement, restoration, or generative priors into fusion [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Although they improve scene illumination and texture, they still pursue source fidelity, leaving the thermal patches on targets intact. For vision models, these patches push the fused image away from the data distribution of visible images, degrading the predictions of detection and segmentation models pretrained on visible images. To address this issue, task-driven methods introduce detection or segmentation losses and train the fusion network jointly with the task network [ 5 , 6 ] . Nevertheless, these methods usually still build on source-fidelity losses and cannot fundamentally improve the naturalness of the fused images. As a result, their performance gains largely rely on fine-tuning the task network on the fused results and can hardly transfer to existing models pretrained on visible images. Moreover, the complementary value of infrared and visible image fusion lies particularly in targets that are hard to recognize in the visible image but salient in the infrared image. Brightening the visible image alone, as single-modality low-light enhancement does [ 7 ] , can hardly recover these targets, as shown in Fig. 1 (e). In other words, making these targets discernible depends on the location and contour cues provided by the infrared image. However, task losses mainly constrain the final predictions and impose no explicit constraint on the contribution of each modality, so the optimization may rely on discriminative features already present in the visible image and fail to fully exploit the complementary information of infrared. To address these problems, we redefine infrared and visible image fusion as natural complementary enhancement . The core idea is to exploit cross-modal complementary cues to generate a clear and natural visible-style image, rather than to preserve and superimpose the information of the two modalities directly. Specifically, the visible image determines how targets should look, providing scene color and texture to constrain the appearance of the fused result. The infrared image indicates where targets are and provides their contour cues, guiding the enhancement of targets that are hard to recognize in the visible image. With the prior learned by a generative foundation model, infrared targets are no longer directly superimposed as bright patches of thermal radiation. Instead, they are rendered with visible colors and textures consistent with the surrounding scene and become clearly recognizable, as shown in Fig. 1 (f). As a result, the fused image not only has a natural appearance that agrees with human visual perception but also lies closer to the data distribution of visible images, providing clearer target information for downstream detection and segmentation models that are pretrained on visible images. To realize natural complementary enhancement, we propose NatureFusion, a generative image fusion framework that uses two decoupled adapters for natural fusion and task adaptation, as shown in Fig. 2 . More specifically, to address the lack of fusion ground truth, we introduce a generative foundation model as a teacher, which generates fused images with both a natural appearance and target discriminability under the joint guidance of the visible image and infrared target cues. Since this teacher is costly to query, we distill its generative capability into a pretrained generative model by training only a light-weight fusion adapter with conditional flow matching. Benefiting from the natural-image prior of the pretrained model, the fusion adapter learns effectively from limited demonstrations and enables natural complementary enhancement from infrared and visible image pairs alone. Building on these natural results, which already lie close to the data distribution of visible images, we further train the task adapter to improve downstream performance. We keep the generative model and the fusion adapter frozen and supervise the task adapter with a frozen detector pretrained on visible images. In this way, task optimization adapts the fused results to existing vision models while leaving the learned natural mapping unchanged, and the resulting gains carry over to other models pretrained on visible images. As noted above, the detection loss constrains only the final predictions, so the task adapter may still rely on discriminative features already present in the visible image. To prevent this, we use the difference between predictions with and without infrared to explicitly strengthen infrared’s complementary contribution. Our main contributions are as follows. • We propose natural complementary enhancement, a new fusion paradigm that converts infrared target cues into a scene-consistent visible appearance rather than superimposing them, serving both humans and vision models. • We propose a fusion learning method guided by a generative foundation model, which constructs fusion supervision from multi-modal inputs and trains a fusion adapter with conditional flow matching for natural fusion. • We design a decoupled task adaptation method that improves downstream task performance through detection supervision and the enhancement of complementary information, while preserving the natural fusion capability. • Extensive experiments demonstrate that NatureFusion generates natural and visually pleasing results and substantially improves the performance of various detection and segmentation models pretrained on visible images.

sections.heading: II-A Degradation-Aware Multi-Modal Image Fusion
sections.text: Under adverse imaging conditions, degradations such as low illumination and noise propagate from the source images into the fused results. To address this issue, degradation-aware fusion incorporates degradation handling into cross-modal information integration. Early methods start by adjusting the contribution of each modality. For example, PIAFusion [ 8 ] uses the illumination probability to adjust the weights of the two modalities in the fusion loss. Later, DIVFusion [ 1 ] removes the illumination degradation in the visible image before fusion, while Text-IF [ 2 ] unifies restoration and fusion in a single model under the guidance of textual semantics. Another line of work introduces generative priors. DDFM [ 3 ] performs fusion using the image prior learned by a pretrained diffusion model. OmniFuse [ 4 ] and DuS-DiFuse [ 9 ] further extend this idea to degraded scenes by jointly modeling degradation removal and fusion in the latent space. These methods have progressively improved fusion quality under degradation. However, they still follow the source-fidelity paradigm, so infrared targets in their fused results appear as bright patches of thermal radiation. In contrast, NatureFusion uses natural fused images generated by a generative foundation model as supervision and renders infrared targets with a visible appearance consistent with the surrounding scene.

sections.heading: II-B Task-Driven Multi-Modal Image Fusion
sections.text: Task-driven fusion introduces supervision from downstream vision tasks such as detection and segmentation to make fused images more suitable for machine perception. SeAFusion [ 5 ] uses a semantic segmentation loss to guide the training of the fusion network, and SegMiF [ 10 ] links fusion and segmentation features through hierarchical interactive attention. TDFusion [ 6 ] learns a fusion loss under task supervision, while DCEvo [ 11 ] balances the optimization of fusion and detection through evolutionary learning. These methods have improved downstream performance. However, they usually still build on source-fidelity losses and thus produce unnatural fused results, and their task losses impose no explicit constraint on the infrared contribution. In contrast, NatureFusion performs task adaptation on top of natural fused results and explicitly strengthens the complementary contribution of infrared.

sections.heading: II-C Single-Modality Image Enhancement
sections.text: Unlike the two fusion paradigms above, natural complementary enhancement no longer pursues source fidelity and instead generates a natural visible-style image. Single-modality image enhancement likewise aims to improve the natural appearance of visible images. This subsection therefore reviews such methods, with a focus on low-light image enhancement. Based on Retinex theory, Retinexformer [ 12 ] estimates illumination to brighten the image and removes the noise in dark regions as well as the artifacts introduced by brightening. HVI-CIDNet [ 13 ] proposes the HVI color space, in which brightness and color are decoupled and enhanced separately, and DarkIR [ 14 ] performs robust low-light image restoration. Generative priors have also been introduced into this field. DiffLL [ 15 ] and Diff-Retinex++ [ 16 ] enhance images with diffusion models, and QuadPrior [ 17 ] and MR. Illuminate [ 18 ] achieve zero-reference and zero-shot enhancement with physical and diffusion priors, respectively. These methods rely on visible observations and image priors to improve visual quality. However, they cannot reliably recover targets that are barely recognizable in the visible image. Image priors can suggest plausible colors and textures, but provide no additional observation of a target’s presence or location in the current scene. In contrast, NatureFusion obtains the locations and contours of such targets from the infrared image, making them clearly recognizable in the visible-style result. sections.heading: III-A Problem Formulation
sections.text: Given registered visible and infrared images of the same scene, I vi ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 I_{\mathrm{vi}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} and I ir ∈ ℝ H × W I_{\mathrm{ir}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} , NatureFusion generates an RGB fused image I f ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 I_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} . Under the proposed natural complementary enhancement principle, I f I_{f} should resemble a visible image captured under more favorable imaging conditions. Infrared reveals the locations and contours of targets that are difficult to discern in the visible image, while the visible image provides scene-consistent color and illumination cues to render these targets with natural visible appearance. Learning this mapping presents two challenges. First, such an ideal I f I_{f} cannot be directly captured, leaving no ground truth for supervision. Second, downstream task adaptation may affect the fusion capability already learned. As shown in Fig. 2 , NatureFusion uses the pretrained generative model FLUX.2 [klein] [ 19 ] as its backbone, with parameters θ 0 \theta_{0} . We introduce two decoupled LoRA adapters [ 20 ] , a fusion adapter with parameters ϕ F \phi_{F} and a task adapter with parameters ϕ T \phi_{T} . Training proceeds in three stages. Stage I uses a generative foundation model as the teacher to produce fusion demonstrations I ~ f \tilde{I}_{f} offline from both inputs (Sec. III-B ). Stage II trains the fusion adapter through flow matching, using these demonstrations as supervision and the image pair as the condition (Sec. III-C ). Stage III freezes the fusion adapter and trains only the task adapter to strengthen the complementary contribution of infrared under frozen detector supervision (Sec. III-D ). At inference, both adapters operate jointly, and only the image pair is required (Sec. III-E ). The person bounding boxes ℬ \mathcal{B} are taken from dataset annotations and used only during training. They define infrared guidance regions for the teacher and supervise detection in Stage III.

sections.heading: IV-A Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets. Following the procedure in Sec. III-B , we construct LLVIP-NCE from LLVIP [ 25 ] . It contains 779 sets of registered visible and infrared images, teacher fusion demonstrations, and person bounding box annotations. We divide them into 536 training, 132 validation, and 111 test samples with no scene overlap between splits. Both adapters are learned exclusively on the training split. The test split is used for component ablations, comparisons of teacher generation with and without infrared guidance, and teacher and student comparisons. Cross-dataset evaluation uses SMOD [ 26 ] , MFNet [ 27 ] , and M3FD [ 28 ] , none of which is used to train NatureFusion. Dataset suffixes denote the number of image pairs. Pedestrian detection and missed pedestrian recall are evaluated on SMOD-200, LLVIP-250, and M3FD-150. SMOD-200 is a fixed set of 200 nighttime SMOD pairs, with the original pedestrian and rider annotations merged into a single pedestrian category. LLVIP-250 is a fixed set of 250 LLVIP pairs. M3FD-150 consists of 150 pairs selected from M3FD. Fusion statistics and perceptual quality are evaluated on 20 pairs per dataset, randomly drawn from SMOD-200, MFNet-250, and M3FD-150, respectively, and shared by all methods. On all evaluation sets, every method is applied without further training, and no evaluator is fine-tuned on them. Frozen segmentation is evaluated on MFNet-250, a fixed set of 250 MFNet pairs (76 daytime and 174 nighttime). For retrained segmentation, the segmenters are trained on 100 additional pairs outside MFNet-250. Removing the 59 pairs of MFNet-250 that share acquisition dates with these training pairs yields the test set MFNet-191. The 100 pairs are used only to train the segmenters, and all image generation methods, including NatureFusion, remain fixed. Compared methods. We compare against fourteen methods. The seven multi-modal fusion methods are Text-IF [ 2 ] , OmniFuse [ 4 ] , HCLFuse [ 29 ] , DSPFusion [ 30 ] , DuS-DiFuse [ 9 ] , DiTFuse [ 31 ] , and ISFuse [ 32 ] . The seven single-modality enhancement methods comprise six low-light enhancement methods, namely Retinexformer [ 12 ] , DiffLL [ 15 ] , QuadPrior [ 17 ] , DarkIR [ 14 ] , HVI-CIDNet [ 13 ] , and Diff-Retinex++ [ 16 ] , together with the single-image fusion method MagicFuse [ 33 ] . We use the public implementations and corresponding pretrained weights. Multi-modal fusion methods receive identical visible and infrared images, and single-modality enhancement methods receive the same visible input. Evaluation metrics. We assess image quality through fusion statistics and perceptual quality. The fusion metrics are entropy (EN), spatial frequency (SF), standard deviation (SD), average gradient (AG), edge intensity (EI), and mutual information (MI), all computed on 8-bit grayscale outputs and reported with higher values indicating better performance. The first five characterize information content, contrast, or local variation in the output, whereas MI sums the mutual information between the output and each of the two source images, measuring its statistical dependence on their intensities. Perceptual quality is evaluated using six no-reference metrics, including DBCNN [ 34 ] , MUSIQ [ 35 ] , MANIQA [ 36 ] , ARNIQA [ 37 ] , CLIP-IQA [ 38 ] , and LIQE [ 39 ] . Higher scores indicate better predicted quality for all six metrics. Ablations and teacher and student comparisons additionally report NIQE [ 40 ] , for which lower values are better. All no-reference metrics use their corresponding default configurations in PyIQA 0.1.16 [ 41 ] , taking RGB outputs as input and applying their respective internal preprocessing. DBCNN uses the KonIQ-10k weights [ 42 ] . All image quality metrics are computed per image and then averaged. Downstream evaluation primarily uses frozen models pretrained on visible images to assess whether fused images can be directly used by existing vision models. Detection is evaluated with seven COCO-pretrained models [ 23 ] , including YOLO11x [ 22 ] , YOLO26x [ 43 ] , Faster R-CNN [ 44 ] , RetinaNet [ 45 ] , Cascade R-CNN [ 46 ] , RT-DETRv2 [ 47 ] , and D-FINE-L [ 48 ] . RT-DETRv2 is abbreviated as RTDv2 in the tables. Only YOLO11x provides detection supervision in Stage III. The other six detectors do not participate in NatureFusion training. Following the COCO protocol, we compute pedestrian AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} as the mean of ten AP values at IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95 in increments of 0.05. We also report AP τ \mathrm{AP}_{\tau} at individual IoU thresholds in the corresponding experiments. All detectors remain frozen, and each detector uses identical preprocessing and postprocessing across methods. Each detector computes AP over the full evaluation set, and Mean in the tables is the equal-weight average over all seven detectors. Unless otherwise specified, detection metrics in all figures and tables are averaged over the seven detectors. To measure whether fused images recover targets missed in visible images, we define missed pedestrian recall R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} . On each original visible image, predicted boxes with confidence scores of at least 0.3 are matched one to one with ground-truth boxes in descending confidence order. A match requires an IoU of at least 0.5. Ground-truth pedestrians missed by all seven detectors form a fixed missed-target set. Using the same matching rule, we compute each detector’s recall on this set for each method’s output and then average over the seven detectors. R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} is expressed as a percentage, with higher values indicating that a larger fraction of pedestrians missed in the visible images are subsequently detected. Frozen segmentation uses seven Cityscapes-pretrained models [ 49 ] , including PSPNet-R50 [ 50 ] , DeepLabV3+ R50 [ 51 ] , OCRNet-HR48 [ 52 ] , SegFormer-B2 [ 53 ] , Mask2Former-Swin-T [ 54 ] , SegMAN-B [ 55 ] , and YOLO26x-sem [ 43 ] . Predictions and MFNet annotations are mapped to three common categories, Car, Person, and Other. We accumulate a pixel confusion matrix over the full evaluation set and compute Car IoU, Person IoU, and their mean mIoU 2 \mathrm{mIoU}_{2} . Other is excluded from the class average, but pixels incorrectly assigned from Other to Car or Person contribute false positives to the respective category. Retrained segmentation additionally reports the mean IoU over all nine classes, including background, denoted mIoU 9 \mathrm{mIoU}_{9} . All IoU scores are expressed as percentages, with higher values indicating better performance. DLV3+, Mask2F, and Y26-sem in the tables denote DeepLabV3+, Mask2Former, and YOLO26x-sem. In all figures and tables, Visible and Infrared are listed for reference and excluded from ranking. Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison with multi-modal fusion methods. Implementation details. Both adapters are trained on the frozen FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B backbone with an input resolution of 640 × 512 640\times 512 . In Stage II, the fusion adapter rank and scaling factor are set to r F = α F = 16 r_{F}=\alpha_{F}=16 , and training runs for 300 optimizer updates on a single RTX 3090 with a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} . Stage III freezes the fusion adapter and trains the task adapter with r T = α T = 4 r_{T}=\alpha_{T}=4 for 300 optimizer updates at a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} . Both stages use 8-bit AdamW, BF16 mixed precision, a batch size of 1, and gradient accumulation over 4 steps. The learning rate is linearly warmed up over the first 50 updates, and the main model uses a fixed training seed of 42. Stage III uses w = 2 w=2 , λ det = 0.05 \lambda_{\mathrm{det}}=0.05 , and λ anc = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{anc}}=1 . The noise gating and gradual activation of the detection loss are described in Sec. III-D .

sections.heading: IV-B Comparison With Multi-Modal Image Fusion Methods
sections.text: This section evaluates NatureFusion in terms of fusion statistics, natural appearance, and target presentation against the seven multi-modal fusion methods listed in Sec. IV-A . Qualitative comparison. Fig. 3 presents four nighttime scenes from SMOD, LLVIP, MFNet, and M3FD, with target and background regions enlarged. Text-IF, OmniFuse, HCLFuse, DSPFusion, DuS-DiFuse, and ISFuse predominantly render pedestrians with the bright appearance of the infrared input. For example, large areas of the rider’s upper body in SMOD and the pedestrian’s clothing and legs in M3FD are washed out, reducing visual distinctions between clothing and body parts. Similar effects occur in the background. Light patches appear on the originally dark vehicle body in LLVIP, while dark vegetation in M3FD appears grayish white or yellowish. DiTFuse better preserves the visible appearance in the LLVIP scene, but the pedestrian in the dark remains indistinct. Its outputs in the SMOD and MFNet scenes are nearly grayscale. NatureFusion renders these targets with visible appearance consistent with the scene. The rider’s jacket and bicycle in SMOD, the pedestrian’s jacket and trousers in LLVIP, the backpack in MFNet, and the pedestrian’s dark clothing and shoes in M3FD exhibit distinct visual details, with target locations and poses corresponding to the inputs. The curbs, lamp post base and bollard, vehicle front, and distant building in the blue boxes also exhibit clearer structure and more coherent colors. These results illustrate the integration of infrared structural cues with visible appearance. Fusion metrics. Table I reports the mean values of six fusion metrics on the evaluation subsets. NatureFusion ranks first in EN, SF, SD, AG, and EI on all three datasets, yielding 15 best results and indicating high information content, contrast, and local gradient responses. DSPFusion ranks first on all three datasets, whereas NatureFusion does not rank highly. This difference also reflects a characteristic of our approach. MI measures intensity-based statistical dependence between the output and source images, while translating infrared cues into natural appearance changes their intensity relationships in the output. sections.heading: IV-C Comparison With Single-Modality Image Enhancement Methods
sections.text: This section examines whether single-modality enhancement can improve both the visual quality of nighttime scenes and the discernibility of targets in dark regions, and what additional information infrared can provide. We compare against the six low-light enhancement methods and the single-image fusion method MagicFuse listed in Sec. IV-A . Evaluation addresses two aspects of natural complementary enhancement, using no-reference perceptual metrics for visual quality and R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} for the recovery of pedestrians missed in visible images. Qualitative comparison. Fig. 4 shows nighttime pedestrian scenes from four datasets, with person and background regions enlarged. In these scenes, brightness improvement often accompanies residual color casts, noise, or local overexposure. In the LLVIP scene, all six low-light enhancement methods retain the yellow cast caused by streetlights. The visible image in the MFNet scene is dark overall. The enhanced backgrounds exhibit pronounced chromatic noise, while large areas of the pedestrian’s light trousers appear uniformly white, obscuring leg contours and folds. In SMOD, HVI-CIDNet washes out the left pedestrian’s jacket and the road surface. MagicFuse renders pedestrians with a grayish white appearance in LLVIP and MFNet. In M3FD, the right pedestrian is almost concealed in the shadows of the vegetation in the visible image, and only the light trousers can be faintly distinguished in the outputs of the seven methods. NatureFusion reduces the yellow cast in the LLVIP scene, producing more consistent tonal relationships between the three pedestrians’ dark suits and the crosswalk. In SMOD, the pedestrian’s backpack, jacket, and trousers are clearly differentiated. In MFNet, the backpack, dark jacket, and trouser folds are readily discernible. For the right pedestrian in M3FD, NatureFusion uses the infrared contour to render a more complete person in a dark jacket and light trousers. Fig. 4: Qualitative comparison with single-modality enhancement methods. Perceptual quality. Table III shows that NatureFusion obtains the best score on all six no-reference metrics across the three datasets. The compared single-modality enhancement methods can only use the visible signal, and brightening dark inputs amplifies noise, as seen in the chromatic noise and overexposed trousers in the MFNet scene of Fig. 4 . In contrast, NatureFusion consistently draws complementary information from infrared images to supply the target structure missing in low-light visible images, maintaining stable performance across datasets. The difference between the compared methods and NatureFusion is particularly pronounced in LIQE, which scores images by measuring their correspondence with text descriptions of different quality levels. On its scale from 1 to 5, the compared methods score between 1.0 and 1.4, close to the lowest level, whereas NatureFusion reaches 4.1 to 4.7. Since such learned metrics derive their quality judgments from natural photographs, this gap also indicates that NatureFusion produces outputs closer to well-exposed natural images. Recall of pedestrians missed in visible images. Table IV reports AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} and R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} averaged over seven frozen detectors on SMOD-200, LLVIP-250, and M3FD-150. Although the seven single-modality enhancement methods use different enhancement strategies, their detection performance remains similar. Across the datasets, the maximum spread in AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} is only about 7 percentage points, and their R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} values remain below 5%, falling below 1% on M3FD. In other words, although single-modality enhancement changes the appearance of visible images, it rarely makes missed pedestrians detectable, because targets hidden in darkness leave too little visible signal for any enhancement prior to recover. NatureFusion recovers 32.5% to 47.1% of these pedestrians and achieves substantially higher AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} than the compared methods on all three datasets, with the largest margins on LLVIP and M3FD. This gain comes from exploiting complementary information rather than increasing enhancement strength. Infrared supplies the locations and contours of these targets, and NatureFusion renders them with a natural appearance that detectors pretrained on visible images can recognize. On MFNet-250, the seven Cityscapes-pretrained segmenters listed in Sec. IV-A are used to evaluate Car IoU, Person IoU, and their mean mIoU 2 \mathrm{mIoU}_{2} . Fig. 7 shows results from the frozen OCRNet-HR48. Text-IF, OmniFuse, DSPFusion, and DuS-DiFuse segment the main pedestrian but incompletely predict the vehicles on either side. QuadPrior and MagicFuse also retain the pedestrian region, whereas their vehicle predictions are fragmented. NatureFusion produces more complete predictions for both vehicles and the pedestrian, with the main spatial layout consistent with the annotations. This illustrates the joint representation of infrared-salient targets and visible scene structure in its fused images. Table VI reports quantitative results with frozen segmenters. The two source images show clear complementarity across target classes. Visible inputs yield substantially better car segmentation than infrared inputs, whereas infrared inputs provide more salient pedestrian cues and perform better on person segmentation. However, existing methods often struggle to accommodate both classes. Text-IF obtains Car IoU close to the visible input, and DuS-DiFuse and ISFuse perform well on person segmentation, but HCLFuse and DiTFuse show substantial drops in Car IoU. In contrast, NatureFusion ranks first in all fourteen evaluations across seven segmenters. Its mean Car and Person IoU reach 68.11 and 66.94, exceeding the better source input for each class by 20.35 and 19.83 percentage points, respectively. NatureFusion also performs consistently across segmenters, whereas some compared methods fluctuate considerably. For example, HCLFuse obtains a Car IoU of only 6.89 with PSPNet. These results show that NatureFusion effectively uses complementary visible and infrared information to improve segmentation of both cars and persons without sacrificing either class. Retrained segmentation. To assess performance after segmenters adapt to each method’s outputs, we separately retrain PSPNet-R50, DeepLabV3+ R50, and SegFormer-B2. The comparison includes the seven multi-modal fusion methods, HVI-CIDNet, MagicFuse, NatureFusion, and both original inputs. All input representations share the same 100 training samples and are evaluated on 191 MFNet samples acquired on different dates from the training samples. For each segmenter, all methods start from identical Cityscapes-pretrained weights, with the classifier replaced by a newly initialized nine-class layer. We use a batch size of 8, 1000 training iterations, and a random seed of 42, and evaluate the model from the final iteration. Table VII reports mIoU 9 \mathrm{mIoU}_{9} over all nine classes and mIoU 2 \mathrm{mIoU}_{2} over Car and Person. NatureFusion achieves the best performance on both metrics for all three segmenters, with mean mIoU 9 \mathrm{mIoU}_{9} and mIoU 2 \mathrm{mIoU}_{2} of 51.83 and 75.00, exceeding the respective second-best methods by 3.29 and 1.70 percentage points. Compared with frozen-segmenter evaluation, its margins narrow after retraining, and all compared fusion methods exceed the visible input in mIoU 2 \mathrm{mIoU}_{2} . This indicates that retraining helps segmenters adapt to fused images and mitigates performance losses caused by differences in input distributions. Nevertheless, NatureFusion retains its lead on all metrics, showing that its advantage comes not only from more natural visible appearance but also from exploiting complementary information from both modalities to provide more useful target cues for segmentation. sections.heading: IV-E Ablation Studies
sections.text: This section analyzes the roles of infrared input, fusion learning, and task adaptation through ablation studies and examines the amplification factor w w for the complementary infrared response. Component ablations are conducted on the LLVIP-NCE test split, using missed pedestrian recall R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} and the no-reference quality metric NIQE as defined in Sec. IV-A . Role of infrared at each stage. Table VIII analyzes the role of infrared information in teacher demonstration generation, student fusion learning, and model inference. Both teacher configurations in Stage I use person bounding boxes, and their demonstrations are regenerated for this comparison. Adding infrared raises the teacher’s R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} from 21.6% to 29.8%, but none of the AP metrics improves, and AP 75 \mathrm{AP}_{75} even decreases. This indicates that infrared guidance helps the teacher depict more pedestrians that are difficult to discern, although the generated targets may still exhibit positional errors, consistent with the observations in Sec. IV-F . The student uses infrared information more effectively. With the same teacher demonstrations, replacing the second visible input with infrared improves all four AP metrics and R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} , indicating that the student uses target location cues from infrared rather than relying entirely on the demonstrations. Adding task adaptation further raises AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} and R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} to 35.61 and 33.9%, respectively. Removing infrared only at inference reduces them to 32.33 and 23.2%, approaching the configurations trained with visible inputs alone. These results show that NatureFusion’s gains come not only from its learned prior for natural image generation but also from effective use of complementary infrared information during inference. Fig. 8: R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} under different infrared settings. Fig. 9: Qualitative ablation of (a) fusion learning on SMOD and (b) task adaptation on M3FD. Fig. 9 further compares missed pedestrian recall on SMOD-200, M3FD-150, and LLVIP-250. To evaluate the contribution of infrared, the infrared-free control uses two copies of the visible image during both training and inference, sets w = 1 w=1 , and disables the anchoring loss in Stage III. With fusion learning alone, adding infrared raises R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} to 28.3% to 41.4%, approximately twice the 12.2% to 22.7% obtained with duplicated visible inputs. Task adaptation adds a further 3.6 to 6.1 percentage points when infrared is available, while the infrared-free configuration obtains no corresponding gain. This indicates that task adaptation further exploits complementary infrared information. Together with the results of removing infrared only at test time (w/o IR), these comparisons show that using infrared during both training and inference improves the discernibility of pedestrians missed in visible images. Fusion learning. Table IX analyzes the roles of fusion learning and task adaptation through six configurations. First, the zero-shot backbone and Fusion-only use identical visible and infrared image pairs and text prompts, with the latter additionally loading the fusion adapter trained on teacher demonstrations. Adding the fusion adapter reduces NIQE from 3.216 to 2.774 and visibly alleviates the reddish road in the zero-shot output in Fig. 9 (a). Detection performance changes little, with R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} rising slightly from 28.0% to 29.2% and AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} decreasing slightly from 34.62 to 34.44. These results indicate that the fusion adapter primarily improves natural appearance by learning from teacher demonstrations, while further detection gains depend on task adaptation. Task adaptation. Introducing the task adapter while keeping the fusion adapter frozen further improves all metrics, with a particularly pronounced gain in missed pedestrian recall. Compared with Fusion-only, R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} increases by 3.5 percentage points, AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} increases by 0.83 percentage points, and NIQE decreases from 2.774 to 2.738. This indicates that task adaptation further exploits the complementary contribution of infrared for targets that are difficult to discern in visible images. As shown in Fig. 9 (b), the infrared image reveals the contour of a person within the smoke, but Fusion-only still struggles to render the body and legs clearly. After task adaptation, NatureFusion produces a clearer body contour and distinctly separated legs. The qualitative and quantitative results together show that task adaptation further improves target discernibility beyond fusion learning. To further analyze the individual designs in task adaptation, we compare three ablation configurations. With w = 1 w=1 , the complementarity loss remains active, but its supervision target equals the Fusion-only prediction without amplifying the complementary infrared response. In this case, AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} increases from 34.44 to 34.85, whereas R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} remains at 29.2%, indicating that amplification of the complementary infrared response is particularly important for improving missed pedestrian recall. Removing the detection loss or the anchoring loss reduces R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} to 31.4% and 31.3%, respectively, and both configurations also have lower AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} than the full model. These results show that amplification of the complementary infrared response, detection supervision, and anchoring work together to further improve target discernibility. Amplification factor. Table X compares the effects of different amplification factors w w on M3FD-150. As w w increases from 1 to 2, overall detection performance generally improves, with all five metrics reaching their best values at w = 2 w=2 . The largest gain occurs in AP 70 \mathrm{AP}_{70} , which increases by 2.64 percentage points over w = 1 w=1 , while improvements in AP 90 \mathrm{AP}_{90} and AP 95 \mathrm{AP}_{95} are more limited. This indicates that amplifying the complementary infrared response mainly improves detection at moderate IoU thresholds, with smaller gains in precise target localization. Increasing w w further to 3 brings no additional improvement in any metric, showing that excessive amplification of the infrared response provides no further benefit. Therefore, we adopt w = 2 w=2 . sections.heading: IV-F Further Analysis
sections.text: Registration errors. To examine the effect of input misalignment, we fix the model weights and shift the SMOD-200 infrared images to the right by 0, 8, 16, and 32 pixels, padding the exposed area on the left with black. Visible images and annotations remain unchanged. The largest shift corresponds to 5% of the image width. We compare NatureFusion with ISFuse and DSPFusion, which have the highest AP 50 \mathrm{AP}_{50} under aligned inputs among the seven compared multi-modal fusion methods. All detection metrics are averaged over the seven frozen detectors. Fig. 14: Mean generation time per image at native resolution on a single RTX 3090 (log scale). Fig. 15: Performance versus generation time (s/image, log scale). Dashed lines trace the best score achievable within each time budget. Fig. 11 shows an LLVIP scene in which the visible image already contains clear person contours. The infrared image is shifted 64 pixels to the right. ISFuse and DSPFusion overlay the shifted infrared silhouettes beside the visible pedestrians, producing spatially separated bright contours. In NatureFusion, the pedestrians’ body positions, head orientations, and walking poses remain close to those obtained with aligned inputs, rather than shifting together with the infrared contours. This example shows that our method remains stable under input misalignment. Table 11 reports quantitative results on SMOD-200. The two compared methods are sensitive to infrared misalignment. A shift of only 8 pixels reduces their AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} from above 31 to below 12 and R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} to below 7%. As shown in Fig. 11 , shifted infrared targets form separate bright contours beside the visible targets, interfering with recognition and localization by the detectors. In contrast, NatureFusion maintains AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} between 32.68 and 36.21 under shifts of 8 to 32 pixels, close to the 35.84 of the original visible input, while still recovering about 22% of pedestrians missed in visible images. This stems from NatureFusion using the visible input to constrain natural appearance while drawing complementary target cues from infrared. Even when infrared is misaligned, the fused output retains the main scene information from the visible input, avoiding the severe detection degradation caused by overlaying incorrect infrared contours. Teacher and student comparison. On the LLVIP-NCE test split, we compare the teacher demonstrations used to construct the dataset, Fusion-only, and NatureFusion, with the original visible images as a reference. Teacher demonstrations are generated through an online image editing API using person bounding box annotations and infrared guidance. Both student configurations receive only complete visible and infrared images at inference. Detection metrics are averaged over the seven frozen detectors, and NIQE is computed on the same images. Fig. 13 shows person locations in the teacher and student outputs. In the red circular inset, the teacher demonstration incorrectly shifts the pedestrian to the right relative to the input. The pedestrian locations in Fusion-only and NatureFusion are closer to the original image. In this example, the students learn appearance from the demonstrations while using the inputs to preserve target layout, showing robustness to the teacher’s positional error. Table 13 quantitatively compares teacher demonstrations with student outputs. Although the teacher additionally uses person boxes when generating demonstrations, Fusion-only and NatureFusion achieve AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} scores 9.08 and 9.82 percentage points higher than the teacher, respectively, with further reductions in NIQE. As shown in Fig. 13 , the teacher may shift target positions when generating demonstrations individually. By learning natural appearance from multiple demonstrations and using location and contour cues from the input pair, the student better preserves target layout and reduces such errors. The pretrained backbone’s natural-image prior also helps improve the visual quality of the generated results. Task adaptation further increases R miss R_{\mathrm{miss}} from 29.0% to 33.9%, improving recognition of targets that are difficult to discern in visible images.

sections.heading: IV-G Efficiency Analysis
sections.text: Generation time. Fig. 15 compares generation time at native resolution for the seven multi-modal fusion methods and NatureFusion. We use ten fixed image pairs from each of MFNet, SMOD, M3FD, and LLVIP and repeat the measurements for three rounds after warm-up on the same RTX 3090. Timing starts with decoded inputs on the CPU and ends when the RGB output is available on the CPU. It includes preprocessing and necessary data and model transfers but excludes model loading and file I/O. NatureFusion processes a queue of ten images in stages with a batch size of 1. We report amortized time per image by dividing the total queue processing time by the number of images. Its times on the four sets are 7.81, 9.19, 16.71, and 29.09 seconds, respectively, corresponding to speedup factors of 1.6 to 2.7 over DuS-DiFuse and 5.2 to 9.3 over DiTFuse. It remains slower than the other five multi-modal fusion methods. Quality and efficiency. Fig. 15 (a)–(d) compares performance and mean generation time across methods on four datasets. SMOD and M3FD use the perceptual quality metric MUSIQ and the fusion metric SD, respectively. SD reflects the dispersion of image intensities and image contrast. MFNet-250 and LLVIP-250 use performance averaged over seven frozen segmenters and detectors, respectively. NatureFusion achieves the best result on all four metrics. Compared with DuS-DiFuse and DiTFuse, it generates images faster while maintaining its lead in quality and downstream task performance. The other five fusion methods take less time but score lower on all four metrics. These results show that introducing a pretrained generative backbone incurs additional computation but allows NatureFusion to use its natural-image prior to produce higher-quality fused images and improve downstream task performance.

sections.heading: V Conclusion
sections.text: We reformulate infrared and visible image fusion as natural complementary enhancement based on the needs of human observers and downstream vision models. The central idea is to use infrared target locations and contours to supplement poorly observed regions in low-light visible images, then combine visible scene context with generative priors to render complementary information as natural visible appearance. NatureFusion connects natural appearance learning with improved target discernibility through offline teacher demonstrations, conditional flow matching, and decoupled task adaptation. The fusion adapter learns a natural fusion mapping from teacher demonstrations guided by both modalities. The task adapter further improves target presentation while keeping the parameters of this mapping fixed. Inference requires only a registered image pair and a fixed prompt. Experiments evaluate perceptual quality, recall of pedestrians missed on visible images, and detection and segmentation across multiple models. NatureFusion outperforms the compared multi-modal fusion and single-modality enhancement methods on all six no-reference perceptual metrics across three datasets and achieves better overall performance with multiple frozen vision models and retrained segmenters. Ablations further show that infrared guidance, fusion learning, and task adaptation contribute to supervision construction, natural appearance generation, and target discernibility, respectively. Together, these results support organizing cross-modal complementary information through natural appearance to serve both human perception and machine vision.

Jianfeng Ding Linfeng Tang Hao Zhang Han Xu Affiliation: Xunpeng Yi, Yibing Zhang, Meiqi Gong, Zhongyuan Wang, and Jiayi Ma Abstract In the absence of ground truth, most existing infrared and visible image fusion methods pursue fidelity to the source images and directly superimpose two physically distinct modalities. As a result, salient infrared targets appear as bright patches of thermal radiation pasted onto the scene. These patches obscure the original color and texture of the targets, so the fused images look unnatural to human observers and deviate from the data distribution learned by vision models pretrained on visible images. Therefore, we redefine infrared and visible image fusion as natural complementary enhancement rather than source fidelity, and propose NatureFusion , which exploits cross-modal complementary cues to infer a clear and natural visible-style image from low-quality visible and infrared image pairs. Specifically, to address the lack of ground truth, we employ a generative foundation model as the teacher to directly generate visually natural fused images for supervision. Furthermore, to fully distill the teacher’s generative capability while reducing computational cost, we fine-tune a pretrained generative model with conditional flow matching through a light-weight fusion adapter. Last but not least, to further improve downstream performance without sacrificing natural appearance, we freeze the fusion adapter and introduce a detector-supervised task adapter that strengthens the complementary contribution of infrared. Extensive comparisons with seven multi-modal fusion and seven single-modality enhancement methods demonstrate that NatureFusion generates visually natural fused images with the best perceptual quality. Detection and segmentation models pretrained on visible images achieve substantially higher accuracy on our fused images than on those of any competing method. Index Terms: Image fusion, image enhancement, multimodal, infrared, generative prior transfer, task-driven fusion. I Introduction Visible images capture the color and texture of a scene, but targets such as pedestrians are often difficult to recognize in poorly lit regions. Infrared images record thermal radiation from the scene and can highlight the locations of these targets, yet they lack color and texture details, as shown in Fig. 1 (a) and (b). Therefore, infrared and visible image fusion aims to combine the complementary information of the two modalities into a fused image that is better suited to observation and analysis, benefiting both human observers in applications such as in-vehicle night vision and vision models in downstream tasks such as object detection. Fig. 1: Comparison with multi-modal fusion and single-modality enhancement methods. Panels (a) and (b) show the visible and infrared inputs, (c) to (e) show the results of degradation-aware fusion, task-driven fusion, and single-modality enhancement methods, and (f) shows the result of NatureFusion. Red and blue boxes mark enlarged person and background regions, and gold boxes show person detections of a frozen RetinaNet with confidence scores of at least 0.25. (g) to (i) Comparison with seven multi-modal fusion methods in MUSIQ on M3FD, person AP 50 : 95 \mathrm{AP}_{50:95} on SMOD, and mIoU 2 \mathrm{mIoU}_{2} over Car and Person on MFNet. Detection and segmentation each use seven frozen models pretrained on visible images. Bars show means, and whiskers show ranges across images and models. However, in the absence of ground truth specifying what an ideal fused image should look like, most existing infrared and visible image fusion methods follow a source-fidelity paradigm, which uses unsupervised intensity, structure, and gradient losses to keep the fused image faithful to the source images. Notably, this paradigm faces a critical challenge, namely that the two modalities are physically distinct. Infrared intensity reflects the thermal radiation of objects rather than their appearance under visible light, so a pedestrian in dark clothing can appear bright in the infrared image but dark in the visible image. When the fused image is forced to remain faithful to both modalities, such targets are highlighted as bright patches of thermal radiation that obscure their original color and texture, making the fused image unsuitable for both human observers and vision models, as shown in Fig. 1 (c) and (d). For human observers, these patches make the fused image look unnatural, especially in low-light and other degraded scenes, where weak visible signals leave the result dominated by thermal patterns. To cope with such scenes, degradation-aware methods incorporate image enhancement, restoration, or generative priors into fusion [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Although they improve scene illumination and texture, they still pursue source fidelity, leaving the thermal patches on targets intact. For vision models, these patches push the fused image away from the data distribution of visible images, degrading the predictions of detection and segmentation models pretrained on visible images. To address this issue, task-driven methods introduce detection or segmentation losses and train the fusion network jointly with the task network [ 5 , 6 ] . Nevertheless, these methods usually still build on source-fidelity losses and cannot fundamentally improve the naturalness of the fused images. As a result, their performance gains largely rely on fine-tuning the task network on the fused results and can hardly transfer to existing models pretrained on visible images. Moreover, the complementary value of infrared and visible image fusion lies particularly in targets that are hard to recognize in the visible image but salient in the infrared image. Brightening the visible image alone, as single-modality low-light enhancement does [ 7 ] , can hardly recover these targets, as shown in Fig. 1 (e). In other words, making these targets discernible depends on the location and contour cues provided by the infrared image. However, task losses mainly constrain the final predictions and impose no explicit constraint on the contribution of each modality, so the optimization may rely on discriminative features already present in the visible image and fail to fully exploit the complementary information of infrared. To address these problems, we redefine infrared and visible image fusion as natural complementary enhancement . The core idea is to exploit cross-modal complementary cues to generate a clear and natural visible-style image, rather than to preserve and superimpose the information of the two modalities directly. Specifically, the visible image determines how targets should look, providing scene color and texture to constrain the appearance of the fused result. The infrared image indicates where targets are and provides their contour cues, guiding the enhancement of targets that are hard to recognize in the visible image. With the prior learned by a generative foundation model, infrared targets are no longer directly superimposed as bright patches of thermal radiation. Instead, they are rendered with visible colors and textures consistent with the surrounding scene and become clearly recognizable, as shown in Fig. 1 (f). As a result, the fused image not only has a natural appearance that agrees with human visual perception but also lies closer to the data distribution of visible images, providing clearer target information for downstream detection and segmentation models that are pretrained on visible images. To realize natural complementary enhancement, we propose NatureFusion, a generative image fusion framework that uses two decoupled adapters for natural fusion and task adaptation, as shown in Fig. 2 . More specifically, to address the lack of fusion ground truth, we introduce a generative foundation model as a teacher, which generates fused images with both a natural appearance and target discriminability under the joint guidance of the visible image and infrared target cues. Since this teacher is costly to query, we distill its generative capability into a pretrained generative model by training only a light-weight fusion adapter with conditional flow matching. Benefiting from the natural-image prior of the pretrained model, the fusion adapter learns effectively from limited demonstrations and enables natural complementary enhancement from infrared and visible image pairs alone. Building on these natural results, which already lie close to the data distribution of visible images, we further train the task adapter to improve downstream performance. We keep the generative model and the fusion adapter frozen and supervise the task adapter with a frozen detector pretrained on visible images. In this way, task optimization adapts the fused results to existing vision models while leaving the learned natural mapping unchanged, and the resulting gains carry over to other models pretrained on visible images. As noted above, the detection loss constrains only the final predictions, so the task adapter may still rely on discriminative features already present in the visible image. To prevent this, we use the difference between predictions with and without infrared to explicitly strengthen infrared’s complementary contribution. Our main contributions are as follows. • We propose natural complementary enhancement, a new fusion paradigm that converts infrared target cues into a scene-consistent visible appearance rather than superimposing them, serving both humans and vision models. • We propose a fusion learning method guided by a generative foundation model, which constructs fusion supervision from multi-modal inputs and trains a fusion adapter with conditional flow matching for natural fusion. • We design a decoupled task adaptation method that improves downstream task performance through detection supervision and the enhancement of complementary information, while preserving the natural fusion capability. • Extensive experiments demonstrate that NatureFusion generates natural and visually pleasing results and substantially improves the performance of various detection and segmentation models pretrained on visible images. II Related Work II-A Degradation-Aware Multi-Modal Image Fusion Under adverse imaging conditions, degradations such as low illumination and noise propagate from the source images into the fused results. To address this issue, degradation-aware fusion incorporates degradation handling into cross-modal information integration. Early methods start by adjusting the contribution of each modality. For example, PIAFusion [ 8 ] uses the illumination probability to adjust the weights of the two modalities in the fusion loss. Later, DIVFusion [ 1 ] removes the illumination degradation in the visible image before fusion, while Text-IF [ 2 ] unifies restoration and fusion in a single model under the guidance of textual semantics. Another line of work introduces generative priors. DDFM [ 3 ] performs fusion using the image prior learned by a pretrained diffusion model. OmniFuse [ 4 ] and DuS-DiFuse [ 9 ] further extend this idea to degraded scenes by jointly modeling degradation removal and fusion in the latent space. These methods have progressively improved fusion quality under degradation. However, they still follow the source-fidelity paradigm, so infrared targets in their fused results appear as bright patches of thermal radiation. In contrast, NatureFusion uses natural fused images generated by a generative foundation model as supervision and renders infrared targets with a visible appearance consistent with the surrounding scene. II-B Task-Driven Multi-Modal Image Fusion Task-driven fusion introduces supervision from downstream vision tasks such as detection and segmentation to make fused images more suitable for machine perception. SeAFusion [ 5 ] uses a semantic segmentation loss to guide the training of the fusion network, and SegMiF [ 10 ] links fusion and segmentation features through hierarchical interactive attention. TDFusion [ 6 ] learns a fusion loss under task supervision, while DCEvo [ 11 ] balances the optimization of fusion and detection through evolutionary learning. These methods have improved downstream performance. However, they usually still build on source-fidelity losses and thus produce unnatural fused results, and their task losses impose no explicit constraint on the infrared contribution. In contrast, NatureFusion performs task adaptation on top of natural fused results and explicitly strengthens the complementary contribution of infrared. II-C Single-Modality Image Enhancement Unlike the two fusion paradigms above, natural complementary enhancement no longer pursues source fidelity and instead generates a natural visible-style image. Single-modality image enhancement likewise aims to improve the natural appearance of visible images. This subsection therefore reviews such methods, with a focus on low-light image enhancement. Based on Retinex theory, Retinexformer [ 12 ] estimates illumination to brighten the image and removes the noise in dark regions as well as the artifacts introduced by brightening. HVI-CIDNet [ 13 ] proposes the HVI color space, in which brightness and color are decoupled and enhanced separately, and DarkIR [ 14 ] performs robust low-light image restoration. Generative priors have also been introduced into this field. DiffLL [ 15 ] and Diff-Retinex++ [ 16 ] enhance images with diffusion models, and QuadPrior [ 17 ] and MR. Illuminate [ 18 ] achieve zero-reference and zero-shot enhancement with physical and diffusion priors, respectively. These methods rely on visible observations and image priors to improve visual quality. However, they cannot reliably recover targets that are barely recognizable in the visible image. Image priors can suggest plausible colors and textures, but provide no additional observation of a target’s presence or location in the current scene. In contrast, NatureFusion obtains the locations and contours of such targets from the infrared image, making them clearly recognizable in the visible-style result. III Method III-A Problem Formulation Given registered visible and infrared images of the same scene, I vi ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 I_{\mathrm{vi}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} and I ir ∈ ℝ H × W I_{\mathrm{ir}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} , NatureFusion generates an RGB fused image I f ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 I_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} . Under the proposed natural complementary enhancement principle, I f I_{f} should resemble a visible image captured under more favorable imaging conditions. Infrared reveals the locations and contours of targets that are difficult to discern in the visible image, while the visible image provides scene-consistent color and illumination cues to render these targets with natural visible appearance. Learning this mapping presents two challenges. First, such an ideal I f I_{f} cannot be directly captured, leaving no ground truth for supervision. Second, downstream task adaptation may affect the fusion capability already learned. As shown in Fig. 2 , NatureFusion uses the pretrained generative model FLUX.2 [klein] [ 19 ] as its backbone, with parameters θ 0 \theta_{0} . We introduce two decoupled LoRA adapters [ 20 ] , a fusion adapter with parameters ϕ F \phi_{F} and a task adapter with parameters ϕ T \phi_{T} . Training proceeds in three stages. Stage I uses a generative foundation model as the teacher to produce fusion demonstrations I ~ f \tilde{I}_{f} offline from both inputs (Sec. III-B ). Stage II trains the fusion adapter through flow matching, using these demonstrations as supervision and the image pair as the condition (Sec. III-C ). Stage III freezes the fusion adapter and trains only the task adapter to strengthen the complementary contribution of infrared under frozen detector supervision (Sec. III-D ). At inference, both adapters operate jointly, and only the image pair is required (Sec. III-E ). The student is conditioned only on the image pair and fixed prompt, without access to the person boxes or counts used by the teacher. III-B , we construct LLVIP-NCE from LLVIP [ 25 ] . It contains 779 sets of registered visible and infrared images, teacher fusion demonstrations, and person bounding box annotations. We divide them into 536 training, 132 validation, and 111 test samples with no scene overlap between splits. Both adapters are learned exclusively on the training split. The test split is used for component ablations, comparisons of teacher generation with and without infrared guidance, and teacher and student comparisons. Cross-dataset evaluation uses SMOD [ 26 ] , MFNet [ 27 ] , and M3FD [ 28 ] , none of which is used to train NatureFusion. Dataset suffixes denote the number of image pairs. Pedestrian detection and missed pedestrian recall are evaluated on SMOD-200, LLVIP-250, and M3FD-150. SMOD-200 is a fixed set of 200 nighttime SMOD pairs, with the original pedestrian and rider annotations merged into a single pedestrian category. LLVIP-250 is a fixed set of 250 LLVIP pairs. M3FD-150 consists of 150 pairs selected from M3FD. Fusion statistics and perceptual quality are evaluated on 20 pairs per dataset, randomly drawn from SMOD-200, MFNet-250, and M3FD-150, respectively, and shared by all methods. On all evaluation sets, every method is applied without further training, and no evaluator is fine-tuned on them. Frozen segmentation is evaluated on MFNet-250, a fixed set of 250 MFNet pairs (76 daytime and 174 nighttime). For retrained segmentation, the segmenters are trained on 100 additional pairs outside MFNet-250. Removing the 59 pairs of MFNet-250 that share acquisition dates with these training pairs yields the test set MFNet-191. The 100 pairs are used only to train the segmenters, and all image generation methods, including NatureFusion, remain fixed. Compared methods. We compare against fourteen methods. The seven multi-modal fusion methods are Text-IF [ 2 ] , OmniFuse [ 4 ] , HCLFuse [ 29 ] , DSPFusion [ 30 ] , DuS-DiFuse [ 9 ] , DiTFuse [ 31 ] , and ISFuse [ 32 ] . The seven single-modality enhancement methods comprise six low-light enhancement methods, namely Retinexformer [ 12 ] , DiffLL [ 15 ] , QuadPrior [ 17 ] , DarkIR [ 14 ] , HVI-CIDNet [ 13 ] , and Diff-Retinex++ [ 16 ] , together with the single-image fusion method MagicFuse [ 33 ] . We use the public implementations and corresponding pretrained weights. Multi-modal fusion methods receive identical visible and infrared images, and single-modality enhancement methods receive the same visible input. Evaluation metrics. We assess image quality through fusion statistics and perceptual quality. The fusion metrics are entropy (EN), spatial frequency (SF), standard deviation (SD), average gradient (AG), edge intensity (EI), and mutual information (MI), all computed on 8-bit grayscale outputs and reported with higher values indicating better performance. The first five characterize information content, contrast, or local variation in the output, whereas MI sums the mutual information between the output and each of the two source images, measuring its statistical dependence on their intensities. Perceptual quality is evaluated using six no-reference metrics, including DBCNN [ 34 ] , MUSIQ [ 35 ] , MANIQA [ 36 ] , ARNIQA [ 37 ] , CLIP-IQA [ 38 ] , and LIQE [ 39 ] . Higher scores indicate better predicted quality for all six metrics. Ablations and teacher and student comparisons additionally report NIQE [ 40 ] , for which lower values are better. All no-reference metrics use their corresponding default configurations in PyIQA 0.1.16 [ 41 ] , taking RGB outputs as input and applying their respective internal preprocessing. DBCNN uses the KonIQ-10k weights [ 42 ] . All image quality metrics are computed per image and then averaged. Downstream evaluation primarily uses frozen models pretrained on visible images to assess whether fused images can be directly used by existing vision models. Detection is evaluated with seven COCO-pretrained models [ 23 ] , including YOLO11x [ 22 ] , YOLO26x [ 43 ] , Faster R-CNN [ 44 ] , RetinaNet [ 45 ] , Cascade R-CNN [ 46 ] , RT-DETRv2 [ 47 ] , and D-FINE-L [ 48 ] .
